note: Fifteen printables, plus 01b — an A3 alternative to the sound-frame mat, made by the same builder and by the Writing Shelf generator at /montree/library/tools/writing-shelf-generator. All adult-facing text sits outside the cards. CUT ONCE: cards butt against each other with no gutters, and every cut line runs the full width or the full height of the page, edge to edge, so one straight stroke of the blade separates the cards on both sides of it. The lines are light-grey 0.25 mm hairlines — they are cut away, so a line IS the card edge — and a small black triangle at the 5.5 mm printer-safe margin marks each line where it meets the paper edge, because a hairline dies in the last few millimetres of any printer. Card content stops 4 mm inside every card edge, so a wandering blade never touches a photograph or a word. Footer on every sheet: “Cut along every grey line · N cards”. Sheets 02, 03, 06, 13 and 14 are MOUNTED on coloured backing card with a 1 cm border, so their printed size is 20 mm smaller than the finished card; 04, 05, 09, 11 and 12 are not mounted and print at finished size. Sheet 14’s backing card is not any colour: PINK for its tier 1 cards, BLUE for its tier 2 and GREEN for its tier 3, because on that sheet the colour IS the reading level. Sheet 12’s word card is the same 60 × 35 mm as sheet 04’s heart word, set in the same face at the same size on the same baseline, so a heart word off the Tray 4 ring and a word out of the Tray 5 tin sit as one sentence on the sentence line.

items.title: Word-card tins — three tier tins and a free set, 88 cards, 28 mm tall
items.note: FOUR SETS, NOT ONE TIN, and every word printed at the size the child WRITES it. Three SELF-CONTAINED tier tins — pink 13 cards, blue 11, green 15 — each holding every word its own six sentence cards (sheet 14) need, in the greatest number any single sentence of that tier needs at once, so a word shared across tiers is simply printed again in each tin and no tin can be half of a sentence. The fourth set is UNCOLOURED and is for FREE COMPOSITION: the 39 reader words no sentence card uses, plus 10 blanks, so the tin grows as the readers do. THE CARD IS MEASURED, not fixed: its width is the word's own INK width plus G — the ink width of a lowercase `o` at the printed size, 5.909 mm or 0.44 em — to the nearest 0.1 mm, with exactly G/2 of paper each side of the word, so `a` is an 11.2 mm sliver and `penguin` is 50.1 mm. Butt any two cards and the space from the last ink of one word to the first ink of the next is G, whatever letters meet. It is measured on the glyph OUTLINES and not on the advance box: the advance carries each glyph's side bearings, and padding by it holds the paper constant while the space the eye reads swings from 2.85 to 6.17 mm. One letter of paper is the space a hand actually leaves, and it is the spacing he then copies into his book. The old 60 × 35 mm card gave `a` and `splash` the same width and taught him to leave gigantic uneven gaps. THE X-HEIGHT IS 6.6 mm EXACTLY — the ruled line of sheet 15's writing book — solved from the Comic Neue TTF's own OS/2.sxHeight (38.4161 pt) and verified by rasterising a probe glyph, never guessed, so a word he picks out of the tin and the word he writes under it are the same size. Comic Neue is sheets 13/14/15's face, not sheet 04's Fredoka: the tin is a WRITING material now. THE TIER COLOUR IS THE BASELINE — a 0.5 mm rule running the full width of the card, edge to edge, with the word drawn over it so descenders cross it as they do on ruled paper; butted cards join their rules into ONE continuous coloured line under the whole sentence. The free set's rule is a neutral charcoal, the absence of a tier and not a fourth one. No frame, no tint, no label. THE PART-OF-SPEECH MARK IS ON THE BACK OF THE CARD, and that is a teaching decision, not a layout one: with the mark on the front, laying Tray 8's grammar symbols over a built sentence is a naming exercise, because the card has already given the answer. On the back, he lays his own symbols, turns the cards over, and the card tells him whether he was right — the card is its own control of error, and sorting back into the tin still works because he flips. It is DEAD CENTRE on that face, both axes, not inset from a corner: a 1–2 mm duplex misregistration is glaring on a mark 3 mm off the corner of an 11 mm card and invisible on one in the middle. Nothing else is on the back — no word, no rule, no caption, no cut line — and the mark sizes are constant across every card, taken off the narrowest card in the build, because the circle and the dot are the same shape and the size is what keeps them apart. Black triangle = naming, red circle = doing, grey dot = small, Tray 8's shapes unchanged. SO THE SHEET IS DUPLEX, FLIP ON THE SHORT EDGE (the set's convention): (x, y) -> (x, H - y), so a back page carries its cards at the same x, in the same order and at the same widths, strips mirrored top to bottom, each mark drawn 180 degrees round in the back page's frame so it stands up once the card is turned. check() simulates the flip card by card and refuses to build unless every front card is backed by one of identical width in the mirrored position, so pages come in front/back pairs: 88 cards are 10 pages on 5 sheets. The sheet is laid in 28 mm STRIPS, not a grid, because the cards are no longer one width; one tin to a page run, in tray order, and a page never mixes tins. What is in each tin is DERIVED from SENTENCE_BUILDER_CARDS in lib/montree/dark-phonics/writing-shelf-language.ts and the build refuses to run if the mirror has drifted. Sort by the coloured rule into its tin, then by the corner mark inside it.
items.cut: Cut along every grey line on the FRONT (the back carries no cut line) → 88 cards, 28 mm tall and 11.2–50.1 mm wide. The cards are NOT a grid: a 28 mm strip holds cards butted left to right until the next one will not fit, strips are 8 mm apart, and each strip is bounded top and bottom by a full-width cut line with a triangle at each end. The vertical between two cards is a TICK — the same grey hairline running the height of its own strip and 3.5 mm out into the gutter above and below, where the blade picks it up — because a full-height vertical would run through the middle of the cards in every other strip. Cut the strips off the sheet first, then cut each strip into cards on its ticks. 13 pink, 11 blue, 15 green and 49 uncoloured (39 reader words + 10 blanks).
items.howToPrint: Print 5 sheets DUPLEX, flip on SHORT EDGE, 100% on card — 10 pages, front and back in front/back pairs. LAMINATE each sheet, THEN cut; the cut guides are on the front only, and a sheet held up to the light should show every mark in the middle of its own card. One tin to a sheet run, in tray order — pink, blue, green, then the free set — so a sheet never mixes tins and each can go onto its own colour of stock. Sort by the COLOURED RULE on the front into four tins: 13 pink, 11 blue, 15 green and 49 uncoloured for free composition. Then flip: the mark centred on the BACK sorts each card into one of three compartments — black triangle = naming word, red circle = doing word, grey dot = small word.

items.title: Story starter cards ×14 — 80 × 120 mm
items.note: The supplement that unsticks Tray 5. A child who can read every card in the tin can still sit in front of an empty sentence line, because inventing a sentence out of nothing is a bigger leap than reading one. He pulls a card, says what he sees, builds THAT out of the tin — and then turns the card over. The back carries the one decodable sentence the picture is of, so the card corrects him itself and no adult has to be standing there. Not tied to any one lesson: it is on the tray all year. Same card as sheets 02 and 03 — 80 × 120 mm printed, mounted on coloured backing card to 100 × 140 — because these are picked up and physically TURNED, which is what a flip card is for. THE SENTENCE IS LOWER CASE and set in Comic Neue — teacher review of the printed proofs, 2026-09-12. These are the literal words a four-year-old says when he looks at the picture (“hen in a pen”, not “Hen in a pen”); the capital and the full stop are his to add with a punctuation tile off the tray. Comic Neue is the free SIL-OFL face metrically similar to Comic Sans MS, which is Microsoft-licensed and cannot be embedded in a PDF the shelf ships; adult text in the margin is still Andika. THE CARD FRAME IS NEW, and it is the whole of the second round of proofs (2026-09-12): the 1.5 mm square-cornered rule printed as a thin line floating in a large white margin — “a line someone drew” — rather than as a designed card. It is now a ROUNDED DOUBLE FRAME, identical on sheets 13 and 14 and imported constant for constant so the two decks cannot drift: 2.6 mm of stroke with a 5 mm outer corner radius, its OUTER edge 4 mm off the cut line on all four sides so the bleed the blade works into is even the whole way round, and a 0.4 mm hairline of the same colour 2.2 mm inside it, cornered to match. The double rule is the playing-card and certificate cue. Content sits 0.8 mm inside the hairline, square on all four sides, in a 60 × 100 mm box. EVERY ONE OF THE FOURTEEN IS FRAMED, on both faces, AND THE FRAME COLOUR IS THE READING TIER — sheet 14’s Montessori pink / blue / green, the three hexes imported from that sheet’s builder so they cannot drift. The deck used to be framed in a neutral warm charcoal with “hen in a pen” alone in pink, and a neutral says nothing: a child cannot sort the tray by it and a teacher cannot hand out a level with it. Each card is now read against the classroom’s own three-colour code on the words printed on its back. PINK (#D45B86) is every content word a pure three-letter CVC, one sound a letter, and it takes TEN of the fourteen: cat on a mat, pig in a wig, hen in a pen, dog on a log, fox in a box, bug on a rug, rat in a hat, nut in a hut, ant on a pan, cub in a tub — “ant” is filed with the three-letter short-vowel words, and so are “fox” and “box”, the x notwithstanding. BLUE (#2F5FA6) is four letters or more with no consonant blend, and it takes NONE: every card on this deck that leaves three-letter CVC behind leaves it for a blend. The tier is wired through the builder all the same, so a future blue card frames, paginates and labels itself with no other change. GREEN (#2F7D4F) is a consonant blend anywhere on the card, and it takes FOUR: frog in a bog (fr), bee on a tree (tr), duck in a truck (tr), sheep asleep (sl, over the sh digraph). ONE TIER TO A PRINTED PAGE. The deck is ordered pink then green and a page is filled from one tier only, then left short rather than topped up from the next — the teacher prints each tier onto matching coloured card stock, so a mixed page is a page he cannot use. Ten pink cards at four a page is three pink sheets of 4 + 4 + 2, the two blank slots on the third being correct and not a gap to plug; the four green cards fill the fourth sheet. Every page header names its tier on both the picture side and the sentence side. THE GROUND IS PAPER WHITE ON EVERY CARD (2026-09-13). “bee on a tree” is drawn on a scanned textured sheet whose grain runs 226–245 within one picture. This sheet used to white-point a ground by the MEDIAN of its border, which puts the middle of that grain at paper white and leaves the dark half of it below — so the card printed as a soft grey box with a visible edge, the one thing a picture card must not have. It now uses the same paper() as sheet 14, imported rather than copied: the white point is taken BELOW the grain, at the 5th percentile of the border band and floored so art touching the border cannot drag it down, and everything above it clips to paper. Two of the fourteen are white-pointed (pig-wig, bee-tree); the other twelve were already paper and are left completely alone. THE ART IS TRIMMED TO ITS OWN INK AND FILLS THE BOX. The source drawings carry whatever white margin the generator gave them, and on the proofs that margin printed as dead space round a small subject. The builder now measures each drawing’s ink at build time — the box holding all but 0.2 % of its ink WEIGHT at each edge, so soft pencil shading and a light wash are kept while the fading tip of a ground scribble is not — crops to it, gives back an even 2 % breathing margin and fits the result into the whole 60 × 100 mm content box, aspect preserved and centred ON THE INK, which is also what fixed drawings printing low in the card. Every card reaches the full 60 mm width; a wide composition is simply shorter. The source files are never written to. ONE EM FOR BOTH DECKS. The sentence size is no longer a per-card result: 10.90 mm of em, a 7.3 mm cap height — three times the cap height of a reading book — sets every sentence on sheets 13 and 14, and a sentence of three words or fewer sets on ONE line wherever it fits at that em. The old wrap took whatever size each sentence could reach, so “the cat sat” and “the ant sat” set large on one line while “the sun sat” — the same eleven characters — broke to two and came out visibly smaller. A longer sentence takes the fewest lines that fit at that same em, so the deck steps down in line count and never in type size. Holding EVERY three-word sentence to one line without exception would peg the em to the longest of them, “the penguin spat”, at 8.4 mm — a small line of type adrift in a large white card, too timid to be read at arm’s length by the child it is for, and a waste of the frame. Letting that one card wrap to “the penguin / spat” costs one card on one green sheet and buys 30 % bigger letterforms on every other card in both decks. Six of sheet 13’s fourteen and seven of sheet 14’s eighteen take two or three lines at this em; the rest set on one, and every one of them sets at the same size.

items.title: Illustrated sentence cards ×18 — pink, blue and green, 80 × 120 mm

The sentence used to sit under the picture on the same face; teacher review of the printed proofs (2026-09-12) sent that back, because a picture with its words beside it is a LABEL and the child reads the words and stops looking. FRONT = the picture and nothing else, BACK = the sentence and nothing else: the Montessori three-part card, and sheet 13's structure exactly. Its header reads “blue”, which names the group on it. The card carries NO written difficulty label, exactly as a pink-series card has never had “pink series” printed on it: ONE EVEN COLOUR FRAME round the content, the same on both faces and the same width on all four sides, is the whole signal. The solid colour bar that used to run along the top of the card is gone — it was the top of the border, and on the proof it read, correctly, as a border thicker on one side than the others. Mount tier 1 on PINK card, tier 2 on BLUE and tier 3 on GREEN and the tray sorts itself. The double rule is the playing-card and certificate cue. Content sits 0.8 mm inside the hairline, square on all four sides, in a 60 × 100 mm box. Same 80 × 120 card as sheets 02, 03 and 13, so it takes the same 100 mm stands, and the same SHORT-EDGE duplex registration. Fifteen of the eighteen pictures are REUSED art — the Dark Phonics picture books (the-sat’s flashcard tiles, the-sad, the-hot, the-nap, the-dig, the-spat), the satpin-v2 story starters, the satpin-v2 CVC set (w08-sand), and fox-box, which is the same drawing sheet 13 already prints; only green’s blob, crab and jump were drawn for it, and they live in phonics-images/satpin-v2/blends/. Sheet 12 has since grown sun, hot and digs, so every pink and blue sentence can now be BUILT out of the tin as well as read. Tier 3’s blend words (star, penguin, blob, crab, dad, sand, jump) are outside the tin by design — a blend is past where the tin stops — so the green cards are reading-and-copying work; see SENTENCE_BUILDER_GAPS. ONE GROUP TO A SHEET (2026-09-13), so each sheet prints onto its own colour of card stock: eighteen cards are SIX sheets (twelve pages, duplex) — pink on sheets 1–2 (4 + 2), blue on sheets 3–4 (4 + 2), green on sheets 5–6 (4 + 2). Each group's second sheet carries TWO cards and two blank slots; those six blanks are deliberate and are never topped up from the next group. items.howToPrint: Print 6 sheets DUPLEX, flip on SHORT EDGE, 100% in colour on card; four 80 × 120 mm cards per sheet, the picture on the front and its sentence on the back. EACH SHEET IS ONE GROUP and its header says which — pink sheets 1–2, blue 3–4, green 5–6 — so print each pair onto that group's colour of card stock. items.title: My Writing Book — A5 booklet, 18 work pages, one a card
items.note: THE STEP THE SHELF WAS MISSING, and what replaces sheet 05's blank strips on Tray 5. A loose ruled strip is silent: the child builds “the cat digs”, picks up a strip, and nothing on it says which sentence he is writing, so the strip became handwriting practice and was thrown away afterwards. THIS BOOK IS HIS OWN — his name goes in the plate on the cover — and every one of sheet 14's eighteen cards has a page in it carrying THAT CARD'S PICTURE, so the work closes at both ends: draw a card → build it from the tin (sheet 12) → find that picture in MY book → write the sentence under it → check it against the card back. 24 A5 pages: cover with the bookplate, a tracker, 18 work pages, a words page and a finishing page. NOTHING IS PRINTED ON THE LINES — no sentence, no model, no word bank, no card number: the model is the line of word cards lying in front of him, and a model printed on the page would make the tiles ornamental and turn the work into copying. The rule is the school three-line rule ported from build_tracing.py — dotted headline, dashed midline, solid baseline, u = 6.6 mm — which is the x-height sheet 12's word cards are printed at, so a word out of the tin is exactly the size of the word he writes under it. THE TIER IS A COLOUR AND NOTHING ELSE: a small coloured tab on each page's fore-edge, high for pink, middle for blue, low for green, so the closed book shows three blocks down its edge and he opens at his own colour without reading a word. Colours are sheet 14's TIER_C, imported. The picture band is fixed at 85 mm on every work page whatever the rule count, so the book reads as one book and not as eighteen layouts. IT IS PRINTED, FOLDED AND STAPLED, NOT CUT: six A4 landscape sheets, duplex on the SHORT edge, nested with sheet 1 outermost, folded on the centre and stapled twice through the fold — build_booklets.py's imposition, folio, bookplate and print note, imported and not copied, so it is the same physical object as the readers on the same shelf. THE CHILD KEEPS IT: it goes home with him when all eighteen pages are written, and not before, which is why page 3 is a tracker and page 23 is a finishing page rather than a blank. The art is sheet 14's PREPARED art (.build/sentence-builder/<slug>.jpg), never the source PNGs, so the picture on the page and the picture on the card cannot drift; run sheet 14 first if .build/ is empty. 15-writing-book-reading.pdf is the same 24 pages in READING order, A5, for proofing on screen — do not print that one. Builder scripts/curriculum/writing-shelf/build_15_writing_book.py. Sheets 01–11 and 13–14 are untouched.
items.cut: No cutting at all — this is the one sheet on the shelf with no cut line on it. Print the six A4 landscape sheets, NEST them (sheet 1 outermost, sheet 6 innermost), fold the nested stack once on the centre line — the two short black tick marks at the head and foot of sheet 1 mark it — and staple twice through the fold, about 40 mm either side of the middle. A long-arm stapler reaches; a normal one does not, so fold, open flat, staple from the outside into a block of card and close it. 24 A5 pages, 18 of them work pages.
items.howToPrint: Print 6 sheets DUPLEX, flip on SHORT EDGE, 100% in colour, A4 landscape on 120–160 gsm paper — heavier than a reader because he writes on both sides of it. Do NOT laminate. Hold sheet 1 up to the light before folding: the centre ticks at the head and foot should sit over one another on both faces. One book per child, and write his name on the cover plate before he opens it.
